editionStmt.p: The five Ethiopian manuscripts belonging to the Ferdinando Martini collection at the Forteguerriana Library in Pistoia were digitized in May–June 2018 by Antonella Brita, Karsten Helmholz, and Susanne Hummel, as part of a cooperative project for the documentation and digitization of Ethiopian manuscript collections in Italian libraries—including the non-invasive sampling of materials for scientific analysis—directed by Alessandro Bausi (University of Hamburg) and coordinated by Antonella Brita (University of Hamburg and, since 2021, the University of Florence). The project was conducted under the auspices of the Hiob Ludolf Centre for Ethiopian and Eritrean Studies (HLCEES) and the Centre for the Study of Manuscript Cultures (CSMC) at the University of Hamburg. This initiative was funded by the Centre for the Study of Manuscript Cultures (CSMC); by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) through the project (TP C05) ‘“Parchment Saints” – The Making of Ethiopian Hagiographic Manuscripts: Matter and Devotion in Manuscript Practices of Medieval and Pre-Modern Ethiopia’—part of the cooperative research unit (Sonderforschungsbereich) 950 ‘Manuskriptkulturen in Asien, Afrika und Europa’ at the University of Hamburg (2015–2019); and by the European Research Council under the European Union’s Seventh Framework Programme (FP7/2007–2013) IDEAS, Advanced Grant Agreement No. 338756, for the project ‘TraCES – From Translation to Creation: Changes in Ethiopic Style and Lexicon from Late Antiquity to the Middle Ages’ at the University of Hamburg (2014–2019). The initial cataloguing was carried out for the CaNaMEI project by Massimo Villa (philological part) and Giulia Bottari (codicological part), University of Naples L'Orientale, and converted to the Bm format (see Revision history).

It was begun in the month of Yäkkatit and finished in the month of Näḥase, while our king was Zärʾa Yaʿqob and metropolitan Abba Bärtälomewos, and the one who had it written was Abunä Gäbrä Maryam. May the Lord write his name on a golden pillar with a jeweled ink in the Heavenly Jerusalem, together with all his [spiritual] children, forever and ever, amen. Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua were written by Mälkä Ṣedeq, and the rest [I wrote] I, Ṗawlos. If we have added or taken away anything, knowingly or unknowingly, forgive us and bless us, forever and ever, amen. Bless those who produce the parchment, for they have worked hard.

È ornata con 3 figure umane (stanti) la c. 5b, con fregio marginale superiore e con ornamenti ai margini laterali e nello spazio fra le 2 colonne di scrittura sono ornate le cc. 6a, 41a, 93a, 126a, 155a, 174a e 193a”

history.provenance: According to the predominant interpretation of the colophon, the manuscript was produced between February and July 1438 (i.e. year of mercy 90), at the time of king Zärʾa Yaʿqob (r. 1434–1468) and metropolitan Bärtälomewos, in tenure between 1399 and the 1430s. The manuscript was probably produced in the monastery of Däbrä Sǝqwǝrt (Säḥart, Tǝgray; cf. 163-164). Gabra Māryām appears as the commissioner of the manuscript. It came into possession of governor Ferdinardo Martini between 1897 and 1907 and was later acquired by the Biblioteca Forteguerriana between 1930 and 1931. It is mentioned in 81-84.
